title: Boss: the reporting toolkit
summary: Four challenges that combine generics, delegates, lazy sequences and LINQ grouping.

steps.title: A pipeline of functions
prompt: Log lines get cleaned in several small steps: trim, upper-case, replace spaces. Each step is a `Func<T, T>`. You want to glue any number of them into **one** function.
Write `static Func<T, T> Pipeline<T>(params Func<T, T>[] steps)`.
It returns a function that passes its input through every step **in order**: the output of one step is the input of the next. With no steps, the returned function gives its input straight back.
```csharp
var clean = Pipeline<string>(s => s.Trim(), s => s.ToUpper());
clean("  disk full ")   // "DISK FULL"
`params` lets the caller pass the steps as separate arguments; inside the method `steps` is a normal array.
starter: static Func<T, T> Pipeline<T>(params Func<T, T>[] steps)
// return a lambda that runs the input through every step
solution: static Func<T, T> Pipeline<T>(params Func<T, T>[] steps)
template: var clean = Pipeline<string>(s => s.Trim(), s => s.ToUpper(), s => s.Replace(" ", "_"));
Dojo.Eq("clean(\"  disk full \") is DISK_FULL", "DISK_FULL", clean("  disk full "));
Dojo.Eq("the pipeline can be reused", "LOW_MEMORY", clean("low memory"));
var math = Pipeline<int>(n => n + 1, n => n * 10);
Dojo.Eq("steps run in order: (4 + 1) * 10 is 50", 50, math(4));
Dojo.Eq("a pipeline with no steps returns its input", 7, Pipeline<int>()(7));
var counted = Pipeline<int>(n => { runs++; return n; }, n => { runs++; return n; });
Dojo.Eq("building a pipeline runs no steps", 0, runs);
Dojo.Eq("calling it runs each step once", 2, runs);
hints: The method must return a *function*, so its body is `return input => { ... };`. The steps run inside that lambda, not before it.
Inside the lambda: start with `T value = input;`, loop over `steps`, and set `value = step(value);` each time. Return `value`.
As a one-liner: `return input => steps.Aggregate(input, (value, step) => step(value));`

steps.title: A generic cache
prompt: Looking up a price or a customer can be slow. A cache remembers answers so each key is only loaded once.
Write `class Cache<TKey, TValue>`:
- Constructor `Cache(Func<TKey, TValue> load)`: `load` is the slow function that fetches the value for a key.
- `TValue Get(TKey key)`: the first time a key is asked for, call `load` and remember the result. After that, return the remembered value **without** calling `load` again.
- `int Count`: how many keys are remembered.
- `int Misses`: how many times `load` had to be called.
```csharp
var prices = new Cache<string, decimal>(sku => LookUpPrice(sku));
prices.Get("TEA");   // calls LookUpPrice
prices.Get("TEA");   // does not
starter: // 'where TKey : notnull' is the constraint Dictionary needs for its keys.
class Cache<TKey, TValue> where TKey : notnull
solution: class Cache<TKey, TValue> where TKey : notnull
public int Misses { get; private set; }
if (_values.TryGetValue(key, out TValue? found)) return found;
template: Dojo.Try("Cache<string, decimal> loads each key once", () =>
var prices = new Cache<string, decimal>(sku => { loads++; return sku.Length * 1.5m; });
Dojo.Eq("a new cache is empty", 0, prices.Count);
Dojo.Eq("Get(\"TEA\") returns what the loader produced", 4.5m, prices.Get("TEA"));
Dojo.Eq("Get(\"TEA\") again returns the same value", 4.5m, prices.Get("TEA"));
Dojo.Eq("the loader ran only once for TEA", 1, loads);
Dojo.Eq("Get(\"TEAPOT\") loads a new key", 9m, prices.Get("TEAPOT"));
Dojo.Eq("the loader ran twice in total", 2, loads);
var names = new Cache<int, string>(id => "user-" + id);
hints: Keep two private fields: a `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` for remembered values and the `Func<TKey, TValue>` from the constructor.
In `Get`, use `TryGetValue` to see whether the key is already in the dictionary. If it is, return that value straight away.
Otherwise: call the loader, add one to `Misses`, store the value in the dictionary, and return it. `Count` is the dictionary's `Count`.

steps.title: Endless numbers
prompt: Write two **infinite**, lazy sequences with `yield return`.
- `static IEnumerable<long> Fibonacci()`: 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, ... Each number is the sum of the two before it.
- `static IEnumerable<int> Primes()`: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, ... A prime is a whole number above 1 that only 1 and itself divide evenly.
The caller decides how many it wants:
```csharp
Fibonacci().Take(5)                          // 0, 1, 1, 2, 3
You may add helper methods of your own.
solution: for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++)
template: Dojo.Eq<IEnumerable<int>>("the first four primes ending in 3 are 3, 13, 23, 43", new[] { 3, 13, 23, 43 }, Primes().Where(p => p % 10 == 3).Take(4).ToList());
Dojo.Eq("the first Fibonacci number over 1000 is 1597", 1597L, Fibonacci().First(f => f > 1000));
hints: Both are `while (true)` loops with a `yield return` inside. Do not build a list: there is no last item.
`Fibonacci`: keep two `long` variables, `a = 0` and `b = 1`. Each pass: yield `a`, then move on with `(a, b) = (b, a + b)`.
`Primes`: write a helper `static bool IsPrime(int n)` that tries every divisor `d` from 2 while `d * d <= n`. Then count `n` up from 2 and `yield return n` whenever `IsPrime(n)`.

steps.title: Sales by region
prompt: The tests define `record Sale(string Region, string Rep, int Amount);`
Write `static List<string> SalesReport(List<Sale> sales)`. It returns one line per region:
```text
South: 3 sales, 1050 total, best Bo
- the region name
- how many sales it had
- the sum of their amounts
- the **rep** whose sales in that region add up to the most (a rep can have several sales)
Regions are listed with the highest total first. No sales means an empty list.
No loops: this is one LINQ query, with a smaller query inside it.
starter: // group, sort the groups, then turn each group into a line
template: Dojo.Eq("there is one line per region", 3, report.Count);
Dojo.Eq("line 1 is the region with the highest total", "South: 3 sales, 1050 total, best Bo", report.ElementAtOrDefault(0));
Dojo.Eq("line 2", "North: 3 sales, 900 total, best Ann", report.ElementAtOrDefault(1));
Dojo.Eq("line 3", "West: 1 sales, 100 total, best Ed", report.ElementAtOrDefault(2));
Dojo.Eq("no sales gives an empty report", 0, SalesReport(new List<Sale>()).Count);
Dojo.Eq("a single sale", new List<string> { "East: 1 sales, 40 total, best Flo" }, SalesReport(new List<Sale> { new("East", "Flo", 40) }));
record Sale(string Region, string Rep, int Amount);
hints: Outer query: `GroupBy(s => s.Region)`, then `OrderByDescending(g => g.Sum(s => s.Amount))`, then `Select` each group `g` into a string, then `ToList()`.
Inside the `Select`, `g` is the sales of one region. `g.Key`, `g.Count()` and `g.Sum(s => s.Amount)` give the first three parts of the line.
The best rep needs a second grouping of the same `g`: `g.GroupBy(s => s.Rep).OrderByDescending(r => r.Sum(s => s.Amount)).First().Key`. Di's single 500 loses to Bo's 250 + 300.

steps.title: Stage 5: Sidekick's weekly summary
prompt: The same report you just wrote for sales, now for your own time: **`sk summary`** shows time per project, week by week.
Write `static List<string> ProjectSummary(IEnumerable<TaskItem> tasks, IEnumerable<TimeEntry> entries)`:
- group the entries by (week, project): the week is `Sk.WeekStart(e.Day)` (your Monday from *Dates and time*); the
project is the task's `Project`, `(no project)` when it has none, `(deleted task)` when the task is not in `tasks`.
- order by week (oldest first), then by minutes (most first), then by project name.
- one line per group: the week as `yyyy-MM-dd`, two spaces, the project padded to 14, a space, the minutes through
`Sk.FormatMinutes` right-aligned in 8, two spaces, `(<n> entries)`:
```text
2026-11-16  web              1h 40m  (1 entries)
2026-11-23  core             3h 55m  (3 entries)
2026-11-23  web              1h 55m  (2 entries)
One LINQ query; a tuple key `(Week: ..., Project: ...)` groups by two things at once.
starter: static List<string> ProjectSummary(IEnumerable<TaskItem> tasks, IEnumerable<TimeEntry> entries)
var projectOf = tasks.ToDictionary(t => t.Id, t => t.Project ?? "(no project)");
solution: static List<string> ProjectSummary(IEnumerable<TaskItem> tasks, IEnumerable<TimeEntry> entries)
var projectOf = tasks.ToDictionary(t => t.Id, t => t.Project ?? "(no project)");
.Select(g => (g.Key.Week, g.Key.Project, Minutes: g.Sum(e => e.Minutes), Count: g.Count()))
hints: Project each group into `(g.Key.Week, g.Key.Project, Minutes: g.Sum(e => e.Minutes), Count: g.Count())` before sorting, so you sum once.
